cards.b: Roll a ball at a hill without enough speed and it rolls back. A quantum particle, with a small chance, turns up on the far side. This tunnelling is why the Sun shines, how a smartphone stores your photos, and how we see single atoms.

cards.h: A wave does not stop dead
cards.b: A particle is described by a wavefunction. Meeting a barrier it cannot climb over (not enough energy), the wave does not drop to zero inside; it fades out gradually, like sound leaking through a thin wall. If the barrier is thin enough, some wave is still there on the other side. By Born's rule that means a real chance to find the particle there.

The chance falls steeply (exponentially) with the barrier's thickness and height, and with the particle's mass. Light particles like electrons tunnel easily; protons much less; a cricket ball essentially never (its chance is many, many times smaller than one in any number you could write down).

No energy is stolen. The particle does not climb the barrier; it appears beyond it with its original energy, but a smaller amplitude.

In 1928 George Gamow (and independently Ronald Gurney and Edward Condon) explained alpha decay. An alpha particle is trapped inside a nucleus by a barrier, yet occasionally escapes by tunnelling. Wildly different half-lives (from microseconds to billions of years) follow from small differences in barrier thickness. This was an early, striking triumph of quantum theory.

Two protons must get very close to fuse, but they repel. At the Sun's core (about 15 million K) classical physics says they would almost never touch. Tunnelling lets them fuse far more often. Without it the Sun would not shine at its current temperature and life would not exist. Gamow and others applied it to stars in the 1920s-30s.

• Scanning tunnelling microscope. Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer (IBM Zurich, 1981; Nobel 1986) measure the faint current that tunnels between a sharp tip and a surface. It maps single atoms.
  • Flash memory traps electrons by tunnelling through thin insulators.
  • Tunnel diode (Leo Esaki, 1957; Nobel 1973).
  • Superconducting qubits use the Josephson junction, a tunnelling barrier.

In 2025 the Nobel Prize in Physics went to John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis for showing quantum tunnelling in an electrical circuit large enough to hold in the hand (experiments in the mid-1980s). It proved tunnelling is not just for atoms but works for a whole circuit, and paved the way for superconducting quantum computers.

• "The particle digs through." There is no path inside the barrier. The wave simply has some size beyond it.
  • "Tunnelling is faster than light." Debated measurements of tunnelling time have not allowed signals faster than light.
  • "I could tunnel through a wall." The odds are absurdly tiny.

Scanning tunnelling microscopes are used in research at TIFR, IISc and the IITs to study new materials, including graphene and superconductors. Tunnelling junctions are the heart of the superconducting circuits being built in India under the National Quantum Mission.

• Waves leak into barriers, so particles may appear beyond them.
  • It explains alpha decay (Gamow, 1928) and fusion in the Sun.
  • It powers STM, flash memory and superconducting qubits; 2025 Nobel Prize recognised it in circuits.

o: The barrier is thicker or the particle is heavier

quiz.q: Who explained alpha decay by tunnelling in 1928?
quiz.w: A triumph for early quantum theory.

quiz.q: Why does fusion work in the Sun?
o: The Sun is hot enough classically
quiz.w: Classical heat alone would be too little.

quiz.w: Binnig and Rohrer invented it in 1981.

quiz.q: Does a tunnelling particle gain energy to cross?
o: No, it keeps its energy; its amplitude shrinks
